title: Fluctuating Workweek Method: Overtime Rules for Salaried Non-Exempt Staff
description: When a fixed salary covers hours that change every week, overtime is half-time on a regular rate that falls as hours rise. The conditions and the math under 29 CFR 778.114.
keyTakeaway: Under the fluctuating workweek method, a salaried non-exempt employee owed overtime receives an extra half of the regular rate, which is the salary divided by the hours actually worked that week.
notes: Conditions in 778.114: the employee's hours fluctuate week to week; a fixed salary is paid for all hours worked, whatever the number; the salary is large enough that the regular rate is never below the minimum wage; employer and employee have a clear mutual understanding that the salary covers all hours; and overtime is paid at half-time (0.5x) of the regular rate because straight time is already in the salary. Since the 2020 DOL rule, bonuses and premium payments may be paid in addition to the salary under this method. Some states, such as California, do not allow this method. Example numbers to use: salary 900 dollars a week; 45 hours gives a regular rate of 20.00 and half-time premium of 10.00 per overtime hour; 55 hours gives a regular rate of 16.36.

title: Piece-Rate Pay and Overtime: Calculating the Regular Rate for Production Workers
description: How to compute overtime for employees paid per unit produced, including the extra half-time premium and how nonproductive time is paid.
keyTakeaway: For piece-rate workers the regular rate is total weekly earnings divided by total hours worked, and overtime hours are owed an additional half of that rate.
notes: Under 778.111, the regular rate of a piece-rate worker is the sum of piece-rate earnings plus any other earnings (such as hourly pay for nonproductive time) divided by total hours worked in the workweek. Because the piece-rate earnings already pay for all hours at straight time, the overtime premium is an additional 0.5x the regular rate for each hour over 40. An alternative under 778.111(a) lets the employee and employer agree in advance to pay 1.5x the piece rate for pieces made during overtime hours. Example numbers to use: 46 hours, 920 pieces at 1.10 dollars = 1,012.00; regular rate 22.00 per hour; premium 6 x 11.00 = 66.00; total 1,078.00. In many states, such as California, nonproductive time must be paid separately at an hourly rate.

title: Tip Pooling Rules: Who May Share in a Pool and Mandatory Exclusions
description: How tip pools work under the FLSA after the 2018 amendment: managers and owners may not keep tips, and back-of-house sharing depends on whether a tip credit is taken.
keyTakeaway: An employer may never keep employees' tips, and may include back-of-house staff in a tip pool only if it does not take a tip credit and pays the full minimum wage in cash.
notes: Section 203(m)(2)(B), added by the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2018, prohibits employers, managers, and supervisors from keeping any portion of employees' tips, whether or not a tip credit is taken. An employer that takes a tip credit may require tip pooling only among employees who customarily and regularly receive tips (servers, bartenders, bussers, and similar). An employer that pays the full minimum wage in cash and takes no tip credit may include employees who do not customarily receive tips, such as cooks and dishwashers, but not managers or owners. Credit card processing fees: the employer may deduct the pro rata share of the processing fee from tips. The federal cash wage for tipped employees is 2.13 dollars an hour with a maximum tip credit of 5.12 dollars. Several states restrict pooling and tip credits more than federal law.

title: Payroll Record Retention: Mandatory Time Card and Tax Record Timelines
description: FLSA and IRS recordkeeping periods for payroll data, which records fall under each rule, and what regulators expect to see in an audit.
keyTakeaway: The FLSA requires payroll records to be kept for three years and time cards and wage-rate tables for two years, while the IRS requires employment tax records to be kept for at least four years.
notes: Under 29 C.F.R. 516.5, payroll records (name, address, birth date if under 19, occupation, hours, rate, earnings, deductions) must be kept three years. Under 516.6, supplementary records such as time cards, wage rate tables, work schedules, and records of additions to or deductions from wages must be kept two years. The IRS requires employers to keep employment tax records for at least four years after the tax is due or paid (Publication 15). The FLSA statute of limitations is two years, or three for willful violations (29 U.S.C. 255). Records may be kept electronically if they can be produced on request. Many states require longer retention, and a missing record can shift the burden of proof to the employer in a wage claim.

title: Are Training Sessions and Meetings Paid Time? The 29 CFR 785.27 Test
description: When training, lectures, and meetings count as hours worked, and the four conditions that make attendance unpaid under the FLSA.
keyTakeaway: Training and meeting time is unpaid only if attendance is outside regular hours, voluntary, not job related, and no productive work is done during it; otherwise it is hours worked.
notes: Under 29 C.F.R. 785.27, attendance at lectures, meetings, and training programs need not be counted as working time only if all four criteria are met: attendance is outside the employee's regular working hours; attendance is in fact voluntary; the course, lecture, or meeting is not directly related to the employee's job; and the employee does not perform any productive work during the attendance. Training directed by the employer, or required to keep the job, is compensable. 785.29 says training is not directly related to the job if it is designed to help the employee for a different job or to develop skills beyond the job. Time spent on mandatory training that is a legal requirement for the position is generally compensable. Travel to training follows the travel-time rules. Time counts toward the 40-hour overtime threshold.

title: Retail and Service Commission Exemption: Section 7(i) Overtime Rules
description: How Section 7(i) lets some retail and service establishments skip overtime for commissioned employees, and the two tests every pay period must pass.
keyTakeaway: Section 7(i) exempts an employee from overtime only if the employer is a retail or service establishment, the regular rate is above one and a half times the minimum wage, and more than half of earnings in a representative period come from commissions.
notes: Under 29 U.S.C. 207(i), an employee of a retail or service establishment is not owed overtime if: the regular rate of pay is more than one and a half times the applicable minimum wage (10.88 dollars an hour at the 7.25 federal minimum wage); and more than half of the employee's compensation for a representative period of at least one month comes from commissions on goods or services. Commissions can include bona fide commission rates based on sales; draws and guarantees do not turn base pay into commission. Some industries (for example, auto dealerships, which have their own exemption in 213(b)(10)) are handled separately. State law may be stricter.

title: Improper Salary Deductions: Salary Basis Test and FLSA Safe Harbor Rules
description: When employers illegally dock exempt employee salaries for partial-day absences, disciplinary penalties, or operational slowdowns under 29 CFR 541.602.
keyTakeaway: Improper partial-day or operational pay deductions destroy an employee's exempt status across the entire job classification unless corrected under the 29 C.F.R. § 541.603 safe harbor provision.
notes: Under 29 CFR 541.602, exempt salaried workers must receive their full predetermined salary for any week in which they perform any work. Permissible deductions: full-day absences for personal reasons; full-day absences for sickness if under a bona fide sick leave plan; major safety rule violations; or unpaid FMLA leave. Impermissible deductions: partial-day absences for personal reasons, jury duty offsets, or business closures due to weather/shortage of work. Safe harbor under 541.603 requires a written policy, reimbursement of improper deductions, and good-faith commitment.

title: Reporting Time Pay: State Show-Up Wage Mandates and Overtime Impact
description: How California, New York, and Massachusetts mandate half-day or 2-to-4 hour show-up pay when workers arrive for scheduled shifts but are sent home early.
keyTakeaway: While the federal FLSA does not mandate reporting time pay, key states require employers to pay 2 to 4 hours of wages at regular rates when scheduled shifts are cancelled or truncated.
notes: California IWC Wage Orders require reporting time pay equal to half the scheduled day's work (minimum 2 hours, maximum 4 hours) at the regular rate of pay. New York mandates at least 4 hours (or the scheduled shift, whichever is less) at the basic minimum hourly rate. Massachusetts requires 3 hours at minimum wage for shifts of 3+ hours. Reporting time pay for hours not actually worked does not count toward the 40-hour federal overtime threshold under 29 CFR 778.216.

title: Uniform and Tool Deductions: The FLSA 'Free and Clear' Wage Principle
description: How employer deductions for required uniforms, safety gear, cash register shortages, and company tools violate minimum wage under 29 CFR 531.35.
keyTakeaway: Deductions for items that primarily benefit the employer cannot reduce a worker's direct cash earnings below the applicable federal or state minimum wage in any workweek.
notes: Under 29 C.F.R. 531.35, wages must be paid 'free and clear' without kickbacks directly or indirectly to the employer. Required uniforms (bearing company logos or unique colors), name tags, knives, or specialized tools are deemed employer business expenses. If an employee earns 12.00 dollars an hour for 40 hours ($480 gross), an employer cannot deduct 60 dollars for uniforms if doing so brings weekly pay below $7.25 x 40 = $290 (federal), or applicable state minimums ($16.00/hr in CA = $640 minimum floor).

title: FLSA Statute of Limitations: Two-Year Standard vs Three-Year Willful Penalties
description: Statutory recovery periods for unpaid minimum wage and overtime under 29 U.S.C. § 255, proving employer recklessness, and liquidated damages under Section 216.
keyTakeaway: Wage claims carry a standard two-year statute of limitations under 29 U.S.C. § 255, but extend to three years with 100% liquidated damages if the employer acted willfully.
notes: Portal-to-Portal Act Section 6 (29 U.S.C. 255) establishes a 2-year statute of limitations for ordinary FLSA claims. Under McLaughlin v. Richland Shoe Co., a violation is 'willful' if the employer either knew its conduct was prohibited or showed reckless disregard for FLSA compliance. Section 216(b) mandates equal amount as liquidated damages (double damages) plus reasonable attorney fees, unless the employer proves subjective good faith and reasonable grounds under 29 U.S.C. 260.

title: Final Paycheck Deadlines: Termination Timelines and Waiting Time Penalties
description: State-by-state statutory deadlines for final wage delivery upon firing or quitting, and the daily wage penalty formulas under California Labor Code Section 203.
keyTakeaway: Under California Labor Code Section 203, failure to pay all final wages immediately upon termination triggers waiting time penalties equal to one full day of pay per day of delay up to 30 days.
statutoryRef: California Labor Code §§ 201-203; N.Y. Labor Law § 191
notes: Under CA Labor Code 201, fired employees must receive all unpaid wages immediately at discharge. Resigning employees giving 72 hours notice must be paid on their last day; without notice, within 72 hours (LC 202). Penalties under LC 203 accrue at the employee's regular daily wage rate for up to 30 calendar days ($25/hr x 8 hrs = $200/day x 30 days = $6,000 maximum penalty). In New York, final wages are due on the next regular payday (NYLL 191).

title: Nondiscretionary Bonuses: Retroactive Overtime Recalculation Formulas
description: How quarterly, attendance, or performance bonuses must be allocated back across prior workweeks to pay retroactive overtime adjustments under 29 CFR 778.209.
keyTakeaway: When an employee earns a nondiscretionary bonus covering multiple pay periods, the employer must retroactively increase the regular rate and pay additional overtime for every overtime hour worked during the bonus period.
notes: Under 29 CFR 778.208, all payments are included in regular rate unless specifically exempt under 207(e). Nondiscretionary bonuses (production, quality, attendance, safety) must be apportioned back to the workweeks in which they were earned (778.209). If a $1,200 quarterly bonus is earned over a 12-week period with 50 total overtime hours and 480 total hours, the bonus increases the regular rate by $1,200 / 480 = $2.50/hr, triggering an additional half-time true-up of 50 x ($2.50 x 0.5) = $62.50.

title: Bona Fide Meal Breaks: The Relieved-of-Duty Test and Desk Lunch Liability
description: Distinguishing unpaid 30-minute meal periods from compensable worktime under 29 CFR 785.19. Why eating at desks or remaining on standby triggers overtime pay.
keyTakeaway: Under 29 C.F.R. § 785.19, meal breaks are unpaid only if the worker is completely relieved from all duty for at least 30 minutes; answering emails or staying at workstations makes the entire period paid time.
notes: Under 29 CFR 785.19, bona fide meal periods must typically be 30 minutes or longer and the employee must be completely relieved from duty. If an employee is required to answer phone calls, monitor equipment, or remain seated at a customer desk while eating, the break is compensable hours worked. If an employee logs 40 hours of straight work plus five unpaid 30-minute desk lunches (2.5 hours total), the employer owes 2.5 hours of overtime at time-and-a-half.

title: Remote Work Expense Reimbursements: Mandatory Stipends and Tax Rules
description: State statutory reimbursement requirements for home internet, cell phones, and computer hardware under California Labor Code 2802 and IRS accountable plans.
keyTakeaway: California, Illinois, and several states mandate reasonable reimbursement for mandatory remote work expenses; under the FLSA, unreimbursed expenses cannot reduce wages below minimum wage.
notes: California Labor Code 2802 requires employers to indemnify employees for all necessary expenditures incurred in direct consequence of duties (Cochran v. Schwan's Home Service established employers must pay a reasonable percentage of personal cell phone/internet bills even if the employee incurs no added out-of-pocket costs). Under federal law, if remote workers must purchase equipment, unreimbursed expenses cannot drop effective wages below minimum wage under 29 CFR 531.35. IRS Accountable Plan rules (26 CFR 1.62-2) keep reimbursements tax-free.

title: Public Sector Comp Time: Statutory Accrual Caps and Cash-Out Formulas
description: How public agency fire, police, school, and municipal workers accrue compensatory time off in lieu of cash overtime under FLSA Section 7(o).
keyTakeaway: Under FLSA Section 7(o), public safety and emergency personnel may accrue up to 480 hours of comp time, while all other public employees are capped at 240 hours before cash overtime is mandatory.
notes: Under 29 U.S.C. 207(o), public agencies (state, county, city, school districts) can provide comp time at 1.5 hours per overtime hour worked under an agreement with employees or collective bargaining. Accrual limits: 480 hours for public safety, emergency response, and seasonal activities (representing 320 OT hours); 240 hours for all other municipal workers (160 OT hours). Any hours beyond statutory caps must be paid in cash. Upon separation, accrued comp time must be cashed out at the average regular rate over the last 3 years or final rate, whichever is higher.

title: Shift Differential Overtime: Blended Rate Calculations for Night Shifts
description: How hourly night, graveyard, and weekend shift premiums must be factored into the FLSA regular rate to calculate legal time-and-a-half overtime.
keyTakeaway: Shift differential premiums cannot be paid as straight hourly additions during overtime; they must be blended into total straight-time earnings to elevate the base overtime multiplier.
notes: Under 29 CFR 778.207(b), shift differentials paid for working undesirable hours (night, swing, weekend, hazardous shifts) are part of the regular rate. Example: Worker earns base $20/hr for 40 day hours ($800) and $25/hr ($20 + $5 differential) for 10 night hours ($250). Total straight-time earnings = $1,050 for 50 hours. Regular rate = $1,050 / 50 = $21.00/hr. Overtime premium = 10 OT hours x ($21.00 x 0.5) = $105.00. Total gross pay = $1,050 + $105 = $1,155.00.

title: FMLA Unpaid Leave Payroll Docking: Hourly Deductions for Exempt Staff
description: The specific exception in 29 CFR 825.206 allowing employers to dock exempt salaried employee pay on an hourly basis for intermittent FMLA leave without voiding exemptions.
keyTakeaway: Under 29 C.F.R. § 825.206, employers may make partial-day salary deductions for intermittent FMLA leave without violating the FLSA salary basis test or triggering overtime liability.
notes: While 29 CFR 541.602 strictly prohibits partial-day deductions from exempt employee salaries, the Family and Medical Leave Act provides a statutory carve-out in 29 CFR 825.206. Employers may convert an exempt salary into an hourly equivalent and dock pay for partial-day FMLA absences without losing the white-collar overtime exemption. Calculation: Weekly salary divided by normal scheduled hours (e.g. $1,600 / 40 hrs = $40/hr). A 4-hour intermittent FMLA medical appointment results in a $160 salary reduction.

title: Paid Sick Leave Pay Rates: Regular Rate vs Base Wage Calculations
description: How California Labor Code 246 and state sick pay laws mandate calculating sick wages using blended regular rates, commissions, and shift premiums instead of base hourly pay.
keyTakeaway: State mandatory paid sick leave laws frequently prohibit paying base hourly rates, requiring employers to calculate sick leave wages using a 90-day regular rate average including differentials and commissions.
statutoryRef: California Labor Code § 246; N.Y. Labor Law § 196-b
notes: Under California Labor Code 246(l), non-exempt employees must be paid for sick leave using either: (1) the regular rate of pay of the workweek in which the leave was taken; or (2) total non-overtime earnings divided by total non-overtime hours over the prior 90-day pay period. Paying simple base hourly rates violates state law whenever an employee has earned shift differentials, nondiscretionary bonuses, or sales commissions in the prior 90 days.

title: Tip Deductions for Credit Card Processing Fees: Federal Rules and Limits
description: When employers may deduct actual credit card transactional interchange fees from charged employee tips under FLSA regulations and state-specific bans.
keyTakeaway: Federal law allows employers to deduct only the actual transactional fee percentage charged by the credit card processor from an employee's tip, but several states strictly ban the practice.
notes: Under DOL guidance and federal circuit court precedent, an employer may subtract the actual transaction fee percentage (e.g. 2.5%) charged by the credit card company from the charged tip before paying the employee, provided the deduction does not reduce effective wages below the minimum wage. However, states like California, Maine, and Massachusetts strictly prohibit any credit card fee deductions from employee tips under state labor codes.

title: The FLSA De Minimis Doctrine: Compensable Preliminary and Postliminary Time
description: When minutes spent logging into computers, donning protective gear, or passing security checkpoints cross the threshold into mandatory paid worktime.
keyTakeaway: Under 29 C.F.R. § 785.47, insubstantial periods of a few seconds or minutes beyond scheduled hours may be disregarded as de minimis only when recording them is administratively impractical.
notes: Under 29 CFR 785.47, de minimis doctrine applies only where trifles of a few seconds or minutes are in question and cannot as a practical matter be measured. Regular, scheduled preliminary activities (such as boot-up time for call center systems, donning specialized PPE, or mandatory shift briefings of 5-10 minutes daily) are compensable working hours under 10th and 9th Circuit rulings. Employers cannot arbitrarily truncate recorded time.

title: Texas Overtime Laws: TWC Payday Rules, 40-Hour Limits & Exemptions
description: How the Texas Payday Law interacts with federal FLSA Section 7(a) overtime requirements, mandatory pay frequencies, and wage claim enforcement by the TWC.
keyTakeaway: Texas follows the federal 40-hour overtime standard with no daily overtime cap, but enforces strict semi-monthly payday deadlines and wage collection remedies under Texas Labor Code Chapter 61.
notes: Under the Texas Payday Law (Texas Labor Code Chapter 61), Texas employers must pay non-exempt employees at least twice per month (semimonthly) on designated paydays. Texas has no state overtime law or daily overtime requirement, relying entirely on the federal FLSA 40-hour weekly threshold at 1.5x regular rate. Wage claims must be filed with the Texas Workforce Commission (TWC) within 180 days of the date wages were due. Fringe benefits like vacation payouts are only enforceable if promised in a written company policy.

title: IRS Annual Lease Value Table: Company Vehicle Imputed Income Audits
description: How employers calculate taxable fringe benefit income for personal use of employer-provided vehicles using the IRS Regulation 1.61-21 Annual Lease Value Table.
keyTakeaway: Under 26 C.F.R. § 1.61-21, the personal use portion of an employer-provided vehicle is imputed as taxable wage income subject to FICA and federal withholding based on the IRS Annual Lease Value Table.
notes: Under Treasury Regulation 1.61-21(d), the annual lease value of a vehicle is determined by its fair market value (FMV) when first made available to the employee. For example, a $34,000 FMV vehicle carries an IRS annual lease value of $9,250. If the employee drives 20,000 total miles with 5,000 personal miles (25% personal use), the taxable imputed income is 25% of $9,250 = $2,312.50 (plus 5.5 cents/mile if fuel is provided by employer = $275, totaling $2,587.50). This amount must be included on Form W-2 Box 1, 3, and 5.

title: Vacation Pay and PTO Accrual: Hourly Rate Formulas and Overtime Exclusions
description: How employers compute paid time off accrual rates per hour worked, cash out policies, and why PTO hours are excluded from the 40-hour FLSA overtime baseline.
keyTakeaway: Under 29 U.S.C. § 207(e)(2), paid vacation and PTO hours are excluded from the FLSA regular rate and do not count toward the 40-hour weekly overtime threshold.
notes: Under 29 U.S.C. § 207(e)(2), payments made for occasional periods when no work is performed due to vacation, holiday, or illness are not part of the regular rate and cannot be used to calculate or satisfy overtime obligations. For example, if an employee logs 36 actual work hours plus 8 hours of holiday pay (44 total paid hours), the employee has zero statutory overtime hours because actual hours worked did not exceed 40. Standard accrual formula: 80 annual PTO hours / 2,080 working hours = 0.03846 PTO hours earned per hour worked.

title: The $2.13 Tipped Minimum Wage: Tip Credit Mechanics & Dual-Job Audits
description: How the federal $5.12 maximum tip credit operates under FLSA Section 3(m), calculating overtime for tipped staff, and DOL 80/20/30 dual-jobs compliance.
keyTakeaway: Employers taking the federal $5.12 tip credit must pay at least $2.13 in cash wages and pay overtime at 1.5 times the full statutory minimum wage ($10.88), subtracting only the tip credit.
notes: Under 29 U.S.C. 203(m), federal law allows an employer to pay a cash wage of $2.13/hr and claim a tip credit of $5.12/hr to satisfy the $7.25 minimum wage, provided the employee receives at least $30/month in tips and retains all tips. For overtime, the regular rate is always the full minimum wage ($7.25), so 1.5x OT is $10.88/hr minus the $5.12 tip credit = $5.76/hr cash overtime wage. Employers cannot multiply $2.13 by 1.5. Under dual-jobs doctrine (29 CFR 531.56), non-tipped work directly supporting tip production exceeding 20% of the workweek or 30 consecutive minutes requires full $7.25 cash wages.

title: Commission Pay and Draws: Recoverable vs Non-Recoverable Draw Math
description: How sales commission structures, draws against commission, and variable pay reconcile with FLSA minimum wage and regular rate overtime rules.
keyTakeaway: Under FLSA regulations, a draw against commission must guarantee at least minimum wage for all hours worked in each pay period, and unearned recoverable draws cannot reduce wages below minimum wage.
notes: Under 29 CFR 778.117, commissioned employees must receive at least the minimum wage free and clear for all hours worked in every workweek. In a recoverable draw arrangement, the employer advances an agreed amount (e.g. $500/week) against future commissions. If the worker earns only $300 in commissions, the employer carries over the $200 deficit against future commissions, but can never demand cash repayment that drops the worker's earnings below statutory minimum wage for hours worked. In a non-recoverable draw (guaranteed draw), the deficit is absorbed by the employer.

title: Full-Time vs Part-Time Hours: The ACA 30-Hour Threshold & 37.5-Hour Schedules
description: How the Affordable Care Act 30-hour definition of full-time employment interacts with standard 37.5 and 40-hour workweeks and overtime thresholds.
keyTakeaway: While the FLSA does not define part-time work and only mandates overtime after 40 hours, the ACA Section 4980H defines full-time employment as averaging 30 hours per week (130 hours per month) for employer health benefit mandates.
notes: Under the Affordable Care Act (IRC § 4980H), applicable large employers (ALEs with 50+ full-time equivalent employees) must offer health coverage to employees averaging at least 30 hours of service per week or 130 hours per calendar month. For payroll purposes, a standard 37.5-hour schedule (7.5 hours per day) yields 1,950 hours annually ($14,137.50 at federal $7.25 minimum wage). Overtime under FLSA Section 7(a) is not triggered at 37.5 hours; it strictly begins only after 40 actual working hours in the workweek.

title: Payroll Conversion Tables: The 2,080-Hour Chart from $7.25 to $100/Hour
description: Comprehensive reference charts converting hourly wage rates to weekly, biweekly, monthly, and annual gross pay across 2,080, 2,000, and 1,950 annual hour baselines.
keyTakeaway: The standard full-time conversion multiplier is 2,080 hours (40 hours x 52 weeks), yielding exact hourly to annual salary relationships from $7.25 ($15,080) to $100 ($208,000).
notes: Standard full-time year = 52 weeks x 40 hours = 2,080 hours. Shorthand: Hourly rate x 2 = approximate thousands per year ($25/hr x 2 = ~$50k, exact $52,000). Baseline figures: $7.25 x 40 = $290/week ($15,080 annual); $15/hr x 40 = $600/week ($31,200 annual); $20/hr x 40 = $800/week ($41,600 annual); $30/hr x 40 = $1,200/week ($62,400 annual); $50/hr x 40 = $2,000/week ($104,000 annual). When adjusting for 2 weeks unpaid vacation (2,000 hours), multiply hourly rate by 2,000.

title: Texas Overtime Laws: FLSA 40-Hour Threshold vs Daily Overtime Misconceptions
description: How the Texas Payday Law and FLSA govern overtime in Texas, why 12-hour shifts do not trigger daily overtime, and special rules for oilfield and healthcare workers.
keyTakeaway: Texas follows the federal FLSA 40-hour weekly standard with zero daily overtime requirement, meaning an employee working four 12-hour shifts owes overtime only on the 8 hours exceeding 40.
notes: Under Texas Labor Code Chapter 62 and the Texas Payday Law, Texas has no daily overtime statute (unlike California or Alaska). Overtime is owed strictly after 40 hours worked in a 7-day defined workweek under FLSA Section 7(a). Common misunderstanding: working 12 or 16 hours in a single shift does not require time-and-a-half unless total weekly hours surpass 40. Oilfield workers: day rate pay must be converted to regular rate by dividing total weekly compensation by actual hours worked. Mandatory 7-day workweek rule under 29 CFR 778.105 prevents averaging hours across biweekly pay periods.

title: Payroll Leap Year: Managing the 27 Biweekly Pay Periods Phenomenon
description: How the calendar drift creates 27 pay periods every 11 years, employer calculation strategies under the FLSA salary basis test, and withholding impacts.
keyTakeaway: When calendar leap years cause 27 biweekly pay dates instead of 26, employers must either divide annual salary by 27 to maintain annual compensation or keep the 26-divisor and budget for a 3.85% payroll expansion.
notes: A standard 52-week year has 364 days, leaving 1 extra day (2 in a leap year). Over an 11-year cycle, these extra days accumulate to produce a 27th pay date for biweekly payrolls and 53rd for weekly. For exempt salaried employees: under the salary basis test (29 CFR 541.602), dividing salary by 27 lowers the per-period salary (which must still exceed the federal $684/wk threshold), while keeping the standard /26 biweekly divisor increases annual pay by 3.85% ($75,000 salary paid at $2,884.62 x 27 = $77,884.74). IRS Publication 15-T wage bracket withholding tables adjust accordingly.
